questions.prompt: Why are AI features harder to test than ordinary functions?
options: Outputs can vary between runs and many different outputs can be acceptable
They have no inputs
They cannot be called from code
They never fail
questions.explanation: Non-determinism and open-ended outputs mean tests check properties and quality criteria rather than one exact answer.

questions.prompt: Which part of an AI chatbot is usually tested with ordinary deterministic tests?
options: Input validation, authentication, rate limits and the tools/APIs it calls
The exact wording of every reply
The model's internal weights
Creativity
questions.explanation: The surrounding software behaves like any other code and should have normal unit and integration tests.

questions.prompt: Prompt injection means untrusted text (from a user or a document) contains instructions that try to override the application's intended behaviour.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Direct injection comes from the user; indirect injection hides in content the model reads, such as web pages, emails or files.

questions.prompt: Which are reasonable defences to verify against prompt injection in your own application? Select all that apply.
options: The model's tools run with least privilege and server-side authorization checks
Risky actions (sending money, deleting data) need explicit user confirmation
Untrusted content is clearly separated from instructions and treated as data
A system prompt line saying "ignore injections" is sufficient on its own
questions.explanation: Defence in depth limits what a successful injection can do. A system-prompt instruction helps a little but is not a security control by itself.

questions.prompt: A support bot answers correctly in English but, in Spanish, it sometimes leaks internal notes from retrieved tickets. What should you add to the test plan?
options: Multilingual test cases for safety and data-exposure rules, plus a server-side filter so internal fields are never sent to the model or the user
Nothing; English tests are enough
Block Spanish users
Raise the temperature
questions.explanation: Behaviour can differ by language. Tests must cover the languages you support, and sensitive fields should be removed before they reach the model at all.

questions.prompt: To reduce flakiness when testing an LLM feature in CI, which practice helps most?
options: Assert on properties (schema, required facts, forbidden content) and run each case several times, tracking a pass rate
Assert on exact text
Run each case once and retry until it passes
Disable the tests
questions.explanation: Property checks tolerate harmless variation; repeated runs measure reliability instead of hiding it with retries.

questions.prompt: An AI assistant can call a `refund(order_id, amount)` tool. In your test environment, a crafted customer message makes it refund another customer's order. Where is the real defect?
options: The refund tool lacks server-side authorization: it must check the order belongs to the authenticated customer and enforce limits, regardless of what the model asks
The model is too helpful
The system prompt is too short
Customers should not be allowed to message the bot
questions.explanation: Treat model output as untrusted input. Authorization belongs in the tool/API layer, where the model cannot talk its way past it.

questions.prompt: Your AI feature passed its eval set last month. Since then the vendor updated the model behind the same API name. What should your process include?
options: Pin model versions where possible and rerun the eval and safety suite on any model change before rollout, with monitoring in production
Assume the update is better
Only test when users complain
Switch vendors every month
questions.explanation: Model updates change behaviour. Version pinning plus regression evals turns silent changes into visible, tested ones.

coding.title: Property checks for structured AI output
coding.prompt:
An AI feature must return JSON like `{"category": ..., "priority": ..., "summary": ...}`. Write `check_output(raw)` returning a sorted list of problems: `'invalid json'` (stop there), `'category'` if not one of `billing`, `technical`, `account`; `'priority'` if not an int 1-3 (bools rejected); `'summary'` if not a string of 1-200 characters; `'pii'` if the summary contains something that looks like an email (`re.search(r'[\w.+-]+@[\w-]+\.[\w.]+', summary)`).

Example: `check_output('{"category":"billing","priority":2,"summary":"Double charge"}')` returns `[]`.
coding.starter:
import json, re

def check_output(raw):
    # Your code here
    pass
coding.explanation: These checks are deterministic, so they never flake even though the model output varies. Run them on every eval case and in production as a guard before the output is used.
hints: Exclude bools from the priority check.
Only check for PII when the summary is a valid string.

tests.name: Invalid JSON
tests.code: assert check_output('Sure! Here is the JSON: {') == ['invalid json'] and check_output('[1]') == ['invalid json']

coding.title: Pass rate over repeated runs
coding.prompt:
LLM tests are run several times per case. Write `flaky_cases(results, min_rate)` where `results` maps case name -> list of booleans (one per run). Return a sorted list of case names whose pass rate is below `min_rate` (0-1).

Example: `flaky_cases({'refund': [True, True, False], 'greet': [True]*3}, 0.9)` returns `['refund']`.
coding.solution:
def flaky_cases(results, min_rate):
    return sorted(name for name, runs in results.items() if runs and sum(runs) / len(runs) < min_rate or not runs)
coding.explanation: A pass-rate threshold measures reliability honestly, rather than retrying until green. Cases with no runs are reported too, because an untested case is not a passing one.
hints: Treat an empty list as failing.

tests.name: Boundary is a pass
tests.code: assert flaky_cases({'a': [True, False]}, 0.5) == [] and flaky_cases({'a': [True, False]}, 0.51) == ['a']
